In this lab you fit a GEV distribution to annual maximum storm surge at Sewells Point, VA using Turing, then test how the 100-year return level changes when you modify your modelling choices.
The goal is not a single answer but a table that shows how much each choice matters.

## Writing a GEV model in Turing

The GEV log-density for one observation $y$ given parameters $(\mu, \sigma, \xi)$ is

$$
\log f(y \mid \mu, \sigma, \xi) = -\log\sigma - \left(1 + \frac{1}{\xi}\right)\log v - v^{-1/\xi}
$$

where $v = 1 + \xi(y - \mu)/\sigma$ and $v$ must be positive.
When $|\xi|$ is close to zero, the Gumbel limit applies: $\log f = -\log\sigma - z - e^{-z}$ with $z = (y - \mu)/\sigma$.

The function below computes this, returning $-\infty$ when a parameter set puts an observation outside the support.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
function gev_logpdf(y, μ, σ, ξ)
    σ <= 0 && return -Inf
    z = (y - μ) / σ
    if abs(ξ) < 1e-7
        return -log(σ) - z - exp(-z)
    end
    v = 1 + ξ * z
    v <= 0 && return -Inf
    return -log(σ) - (1 + 1 / ξ) * log(v) - v^(-1 / ξ)
end
```

::: {.callout-note}
We use `@addlogprob!` to add the log-density directly rather than writing `y[i] ~ SomeDistribution(...)`.
This is because `Distributions.jl`'s `GeneralizedExtremeValue` throws an error when a parameter set puts an observation outside the support, but MCMC samplers routinely propose such parameter sets and need a $-\infty$ log-density instead of an exception.
:::
